passages.t: The leaven of hypocrisy; fear, and the sparrows
passages.happening:
A crowd of many thousands has gathered, so many that they are trampling one another. Jesus speaks first to his disciples: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy” (verse 1). Nothing hidden will stay hidden. What they whisper in inner rooms will be shouted from the housetops.

“I tell you, My friends, do not be afraid of those who kill the body and after that can do no more” (verse 4). Instead, “Fear the One who, after you have been killed, has authority to throw you into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear Him!” (verse 5).

Then at once: “Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? Yet not one of them is forgotten by God” (verse 6). Even the hairs of your head are counted. “So do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Matthew has these words in Jesus' instructions to the twelve (Matthew 10:26-31), and the note there explains them. Houses had flat roofs, a natural place to call out news. ‘Hell’ translates Gehenna, the name of the valley outside Jerusalem where some kings of Judah had burned children in sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31); by Jesus' day it stood for the place of final judgment.

Leaven was the yeast in bread. A little of it works its way through the whole lump. So hypocrisy, a life played for an audience, spreads quietly. Luke names it plainly. Jesus has just eaten at a Pharisee's table (11:37), and he warns his own disciples first: this can happen to you.

Only Luke has Jesus call his disciples ‘My friends’ here. The warning about fear is spoken as a friend.

Matthew says two sparrows sell for one penny. Luke says five for two pennies, as if the fifth were thrown in for nothing. Even that one, Jesus says, God has not forgotten.
passages.ot:
‘Fear the LORD’ runs through the whole Old Testament. It means the deep reverence that puts God first, and it is called “the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 9:10). Jesus sets the right fear against the wrong one. Fear God, and you need not fear anyone else.

‘Not a hair of his head will fall to the ground’ was an old way of promising someone's safety (1 Samuel 14:45). Jesus goes further: the hairs are not just kept but counted.
passages.hard:
Who is ‘the One who has authority to throw you into hell’? Most readers take it to be God, the only judge with that power. What hell is like, Christians describe in more than one way, and the note on Matthew 10:26-33 sets out the views without settling them.

The warning is not meant to frighten anyone into faith, and it is not meant to sit alone. In the very next breath Jesus says ‘do not be afraid’ and speaks of sparrows. The God who has that authority is the Father who has not forgotten a sparrow sold for almost nothing. If you are afraid of God's judgment, hear the same voice that calls you ‘My friends’.
passages.asks: Jesus warns his own followers first about hypocrisy. Ask where you are playing a part for an audience. Then name something you are afraid of, and put it beside the fifth sparrow: thrown in for nothing, and not forgotten by God. You are worth more than many sparrows.

passages.t: Confessing Jesus, and the sin against the Spirit
passages.happening:
“I tell you, everyone who confesses Me before men, the Son of Man will also confess him before the angels of God” (verse 8). Whoever denies him before others will be denied before the angels of God.

“And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven” (verse 10).

When they are brought before synagogues, rulers and authorities, they are not to worry about what to say. “For at that time the Holy Spirit will teach you what you should say” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Mark and Matthew set the saying about the Spirit right after the charge that Jesus drives out demons by Beelzebul (Mark 3:28-30; Matthew 12:31-32), and their notes explain it from that setting. Luke told the Beelzebul story in chapter 11 and keeps this saying for here, among words about standing firm under pressure. Blasphemy meant speaking against God, insulting what is holy.

To ‘confess’ Jesus means to say openly that you belong to him. To ‘deny’ him means to say you do not. In Luke's second book the disciples are brought before councils and rulers, just as Jesus says here, and the Spirit gives them words. Peter and John answer the council boldly (Acts 4:8-13), and Stephen's opponents “could not stand up to his wisdom or the Spirit by whom he spoke” (Acts 6:10).
passages.ot: God promised Moses, who said he could not speak well, “Now go! I will help you as you speak, and I will teach you what to say” (Exodus 4:12). Jesus makes the same promise to frightened disciples.
passages.hard:
What is the sin that will never be forgiven? If you are afraid you have committed it, this note is written for you.

In Mark and Matthew the sin is defined by the setting. People saw the plain work of God's Spirit, setting someone free, and called it the work of the devil. It is not a careless word spoken once in anger. It is a settled refusal to see God's goodness as good, a refusal that shuts the door on the very forgiveness Jesus offers. Christians have described it in more than one way, and these notes do not choose between them.

In Luke the saying stands next to denying Jesus. Does that mean denying him under pressure can never be forgiven? No. Peter denied Jesus three times on the night of his arrest (22:54-62), and Jesus had already prayed for him and told him to strengthen his brothers when he turned back (22:32). A word against the Son of Man, Jesus says here, will be forgiven.

Many Christians have feared they committed this sin. In 1666 John Bunyan, later the author of The Pilgrim's Progress, described in Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners how he long feared he had committed it, and how he came at last to comfort in Christ. A long pastoral tradition answers that the fear itself is a sign that the heart has not turned hard in this way.
passages.asks: Jesus does not ask his followers to be brave on their own. He promises the Spirit will give them words when the time comes. Ask where you have kept quiet about Jesus because you were afraid of what to say. And if a fear of the unforgivable sin troubles you, bring it to him. The fear itself shows a heart that still wants God.

passages.happening:
Someone in the crowd says, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me” (verse 13). Jesus answers, “Man, who appointed Me judge or executor between you?” (verse 14). Then he says, “Watch out! Guard yourselves against every form of greed, for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions” (verse 15).

He tells a story. A rich man's land gives a huge harvest. He thinks to himself, ‘What shall I do? I have nowhere to store my crops.’ So he decides to tear down his barns and build bigger ones, store everything, and say to himself, ‘You have plenty of good things laid up for many years. Take it easy. Eat, drink, and be merry.’

“But God said to him, ‘You fool! This very night your life will be required of you. Then who will own what you have accumulated?’” (verse 20). “This is how it will be for anyone who stores up treasure for himself but is not rich toward God” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Only Luke tells this story.

The man wants Jesus to act as judge in a family quarrel. The Law gave the firstborn son a double share (Deuteronomy 21:17), and an inheritance could easily set brothers against each other. Jesus refuses to be the judge. He goes beneath the quarrel to what drives it.

Listen to how the rich man talks. ‘What shall I do?’, ‘I will tear down’, ‘my barns’, ‘my grain’, ‘my goods’, and then he speaks to himself. There is no one else in his plans: no God, no neighbour, no family, no hungry person who might eat the surplus. He has done well, and his only conversation is with himself.

A Jewish book of wisdom written in Jerusalem early in the second century BC, Sirach, has a similar picture: a man grows rich by hard work and says he can now rest and enjoy his goods, not knowing how little time he has before he leaves them to others (Sirach 11:18-19). Jesus' hearers knew this kind of wisdom.

‘Fool’ in the Bible does not mean someone with little learning. It means someone who lives as if God were not there: “The fool says in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Psalm 14:1).
passages.ot:
The Old Testament knew this man. “Do not be amazed when a man grows rich, when the splendor of his house increases. For when he dies, he will carry nothing away” (Psalm 49:16-17). The Teacher in Ecclesiastes grieved that he “must leave it to the man who comes after me. And who knows whether that man will be wise or foolish?” (Ecclesiastes 2:18-19).

The same Scriptures also praise wise saving. Joseph stored grain in good years so that Egypt would not starve in the famine (Genesis 41:35-36). Proverbs sends the lazy to the ant, which “prepares its provisions in summer” (Proverbs 6:6-8).
passages.hard:
Is this story against saving money or planning for the future? No. Scripture praises Joseph and the ant for storing up. The rich man's sin is not that he planned, or even that he was rich. It is what the story itself names: greed, and storing up treasure ‘for himself’ while not being ‘rich toward God’. He treated a gift as if it were only his, and he planned a life with no one else in it. He thought his life was secured by what he owned, which is exactly what Jesus says it is not (verse 15).

The book page explains how Luke speaks of money: he refuses both the idea that wealth proves God's blessing and contempt for the rich. This story fits that pattern. It is a warning to anyone who has more than enough. Being ‘rich toward God’ means using what you have in a way that God would call rich: generously, with open hands, toward him and toward people in need. Luke's next words make it concrete (verse 33).
passages.asks: Listen to how you talk to yourself about money. Is it all ‘my’ and ‘I’? Ask what you are storing, and for whom. Then ask one practical question: what would being ‘rich toward God’ look like with what you have this month?

passages.t: Do not worry; where your treasure is
passages.happening:
Jesus turns to his disciples. “Therefore I tell you, do not worry about your life, what you will eat, or about your body, what you will wear” (verse 22). Life is more than food. Consider the ravens: they do not sow or reap, they have no barn, yet God feeds them. Who can add a single hour to his life by worrying? Consider how the lilies grow. Not even Solomon in all his glory was dressed like one of them.

The nations chase after these things, and your Father knows you need them. “But seek His kingdom, and these things will be added unto you” (verse 31). “Do not be afraid, little flock, for your Father is pleased to give you the kingdom” (verse 32).

“Sell your possessions and give to the poor” (verse 33). Make purses that do not wear out, a treasure in heaven no thief can reach and no moth destroy. “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
Matthew has most of this in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 6:19-34), and the note there explains it. Sowing and reaping were the work of the fields; spinning was the work of the home. The birds and flowers do neither, and are fed and clothed.

Luke's version has its own touches. Matthew says ‘birds’; Luke says ‘ravens’. Ravens were among the birds the Law called unclean (Leviticus 11:15), so they were not prized. Even they are fed. And Luke places this teaching right after the rich fool, who built bigger barns. The ravens have no barns at all.

Only Luke has ‘little flock’. A flock is small, defenceless and easily scattered. Jesus speaks to it tenderly: the Father is pleased to give you the kingdom. It is a gift, not something you have to grab.

Clothes were valuable, and moths could ruin them. Thieves could break in. Treasure in heaven is out of reach of both.
passages.ot: God “provides food for the animals, and for the young ravens when they call” (Psalm 147:9). God asked Job, “Who provides food for the raven when its young cry out to God?” (Job 38:41). Solomon's riches were famous; 1 Kings 10 describes his gold, his throne and his court.
passages.hard:
Is Jesus saying that anxiety is a sin? This passage is not a rebuke of people who live with an anxiety disorder, panic attacks or depression. Those are real illnesses of body and mind, and they need care, not blame. Jesus himself was “sorrowful and deeply distressed” in the garden (Matthew 26:37). The New Testament's answer to anxiety is an invitation, not an accusation. Getting help is not a lack of faith. A doctor, a counselor, medicine, one trusted person who will stay. If you have reached the place where you are not sure you want to be here at all, tell someone today, and in the United States you can call or text 988 right now.

‘Sell your possessions.’ Does Jesus mean every follower must sell everything? Christians have read it in more than one way. Some, through the church's history, have taken it literally for themselves: Antony of Egypt heard the Gospel's words to a rich man read in church and gave his family's land away. Many read it as a call to everyone to give generously and to loosen the grip of possessions, without a rule that all must sell all. They point out that in Acts the first believers shared freely and sold property to help the needy (Acts 2:44-45), yet Peter told Ananias that his land had been his own to keep (Acts 5:4), and Zacchaeus gave half his goods, not all, and was welcomed (19:8-9). On every reading the words should not be blunted. Jesus really does tell his followers to give to the poor, and to put their treasure where it cannot be lost.
passages.asks: Jesus says your heart follows your treasure. Look at where your money and time go, and you will see where your heart is. Ask what one thing you could give away this week. And if worry has become more than you can carry, that is not a failure of faith. Tell someone, and let them help.

passages.t: Ready servants; to whom much is given
passages.happening:
“Be dressed for service and keep your lamps burning” (verse 35). Be like servants waiting for their master to come home from a wedding feast, ready to open the door the moment he knocks. Blessed are those servants. Jesus says the master “will dress himself to serve and will have them recline at the table, and he himself will come and wait on them” (verse 37). Even if he comes in the middle of the night, or later, they will be blessed.

If a homeowner knew when the thief was coming, he would not let his house be broken into. “You also must be ready, because the Son of Man will come at an hour you do not expect” (verse 40).

“Lord,” says Peter, “are You addressing this parable to us, or to everyone else as well?” (verse 41). Jesus answers with a story of a manager put in charge of his master's household. If he feeds the others faithfully, he is blessed. If he says, ‘My master will be a long time’, and begins to beat the servants and get drunk, the master will come unexpectedly and punish him. The servant who knew what his master wanted and did not do it will be beaten with many blows; the one who did not know, with few. “From everyone who has been given much, much will be required” (verse 48).
passages.hearers:
‘Dressed for service’ is literally ‘let your waists be girded’. A man wore a long robe, and to work or run he tucked it up into his belt. Lamps were small clay dishes of oil with a wick, which had to be kept filled and trimmed through the night.

Whatever way the hours were counted, the second or third watch meant the middle of the night or later. The master is late. The servants stay awake anyway.

Then comes the most surprising line in the passage, and it is only in Luke. The master comes home, ties up his own robe, sits his servants down, and serves them dinner. No master did that. But this master does. At the Last Supper Jesus will say, “I am among you as one who serves” (22:27).

Matthew has the faithful and wicked servant too (Matthew 24:45-51), and the note there explains it. The faithful servant is doing his ordinary job well when the master comes, feeding the others on time. The wicked one turns waiting into abuse of power. ‘Cut him to pieces’ is a fierce phrase, and readers differ on whether it pictures a terrible punishment or being cut off from the household.

Only Luke has the last part, about many blows and few. Those who knew more are held to more.
passages.ot:
Israel ate the first Passover dressed and ready to leave: “You must be fully dressed for travel, with your sandals on your feet and your staff in your hand” (Exodus 12:11). Jesus' followers are to live in that same readiness.

The prophets spoke against shepherds who fed themselves instead of the flock: “Should not the shepherds feed their flock?” (Ezekiel 34:2). The manager in charge of the household is that kind of shepherd, for good or ill.
passages.hard:
Is this passage meant to make us anxious about the end, always afraid of being caught out? No. The servants in the story are not afraid. They are ready, and the reward for being ready is that the master serves them at his table. Readiness is not a mood of fear. It is faithfulness in the ordinary work you have been given.

‘From everyone who has been given much, much will be required.’ People often quote this about money, and it does apply to money. But in the story it is about knowing the master's will and being put in charge of others. It applies to knowledge, gifts, time, influence and position as much as wealth. It is a warning, first, to anyone who leads others in the church. It is also fair: God does not judge a person for what they could not have known in the same way as for what they knew and ignored.
passages.asks: The faithful servant was found doing his ordinary job, feeding others on time. Ask what you would want the master to find you doing if he came today. Then ask what you have been given much of: time, skill, knowledge, money, influence. What is being asked of you because of it?

passages.happening:
“I have come to ignite a fire on the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled!” (verse 49). “But I have a baptism to undergo, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished!” (verse 50).

“Do you think that I have come to bring peace to the earth? No, I tell you, but division” (verse 51). From now on a household of five will be divided, three against two and two against three: father against son and son against father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against daughter-in-law.
passages.hearers:
Matthew has the saying about division in different words, ‘not peace, but a sword’ (Matthew 10:34-36), and the note there explains it. In Jesus' world the family was everything: work, home, worship, good name, and care in old age. A son or daughter who followed Jesus when the family did not could lose all of that.

Only Luke has the fire and the baptism. Jesus' ‘baptism’ here is not water. It is his coming death, which he will be plunged into like water closing over a person. He used the same picture with James and John: “Can you drink the cup I will drink, or be baptized with the baptism I will undergo?” (Mark 10:38). Luke lets us hear how heavy it weighed on him: ‘how distressed I am until it is accomplished’.

The fire has been read in more than one way. John the Baptist said that the one coming would baptize “with the Holy Spirit and with fire” (3:16), and in Luke's second book the Spirit comes with “tongues like flames of fire” (Acts 2:3). So many readers take the fire to be the Spirit, kindled once Jesus' death is accomplished. Others take it as the fire of judgment, or as a fire that tests and purifies. These can belong together: the same fire warms and refines.
passages.ot:
The household divided comes from Micah, who grieved over a broken society where “a son dishonors his father” and “A man’s enemies are the members of his own household” (Micah 7:6). Jesus does not say that such breaking is good. He says his coming will bring it, because people will answer him differently, even in one home.

Isaiah had called the coming king “Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9:6).
passages.hard:
How does ‘not peace, but division’ fit the Prince of Peace? The angels at his birth sang of “peace to men on whom His favor rests” (2:14), and Jesus wept that Jerusalem did not know what would bring it peace (19:42). The peace he brings is real. But it is peace with God, and it does not come by everyone agreeing to leave him out. Where some follow him and others do not, even in one family, a line appears. Jesus is describing that result honestly, not wishing it.

This is a picture of division, not a call to violence. He never told his followers to fight for him. When one of them struck with a sword on the night of his arrest, Jesus said, “No more of this!” and healed the wounded man's ear (22:51). No one may use this passage to justify harming anyone, inside a family or outside it. Nor is it a command to cut off your family. Paul tells believers, “If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone” (Romans 12:18). The division comes from others' response to Jesus, not from his followers' hostility.

If your family has rejected you for your faith, you are not alone, and you have not failed. The psalmist wrote, “Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me” (Psalm 27:10). Keep loving them, keep the door open as far as you safely can, and find a church family who will stand with you. If rejection has turned into threats or harm, seeking safety is not disloyalty to Jesus. Please speak to someone you trust, and if you are in danger, contact the police or a crisis line.
passages.asks: Jesus felt the weight of what lay ahead, and he went toward it. Ask what following him has cost you with people you love, or what it might cost. And ask whether any division in your life comes from loyalty to Jesus, or only from your own harshness. The first may be unavoidable. The second is yours to mend.

passages.t: Reading the sky, and settling on the way
passages.happening:
Jesus turns to the crowds. When you see a cloud rising in the west, you say, ‘A shower is coming’, and it comes. When the south wind blows, you say, ‘It will be hot’, and it is. “You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of the earth and sky. Why don’t you know how to interpret the present time?” (verse 56).

“And why don’t you judge for yourselves what is right?” (verse 57). If someone is taking you to court, make every effort to settle with him on the way, or the judge will hand you to the officer, and the officer will throw you into prison. “I tell you, you will not get out until you have paid the very last penny” (verse 59).
passages.hearers:
Jesus uses the weather everyone in the land knew. To the west lies the Mediterranean Sea, so clouds from the west bring rain. To the south lies desert, so a south wind brings heat. Any farmer could read those signs.

The ‘present time’ is the moment they are living in: God's kingdom has come near in Jesus. They can read the sky but not that.

Matthew has the saying about settling with an opponent in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:25-26), as advice about making peace with a brother. Luke puts it here as a picture of urgency. You are on the way to court. The case is not yet decided. Settle now, while there is still time.

The ‘last penny’ is a lepton, the smallest coin there was, the kind the poor widow gave in the temple (21:2).
passages.ot: The prophets also said the people could not read God's time. “Even the stork in the sky knows her appointed seasons”, Jeremiah said, “but My people do not know the requirements of the LORD” (Jeremiah 8:7). And Proverbs gives the same advice about court: “do not bring hastily to court” (Proverbs 25:8).
passages.hard: Who is the opponent, and what is the prison? Jesus tells it as a picture, not a lesson in law. Many readers take the opponent to stand for anyone we are in the wrong with, and the judge to point to God's judgment, toward which every life is moving. Others read it more simply: settle your quarrels with people while you can, because delay makes everything worse. Both readings agree on the main point. The time to put things right is now, on the way.
passages.asks: You can tell when it will rain. Can you tell what God is doing in your life now? Ask whether there is a quarrel you have been leaving for later, with God or with someone else. Jesus says: settle it on the way. Do not wait for the courtroom.
